input: In order for a sample of an effluent stream to be genuinely useful, it must be representative of the stream as a whole, and achieving this is by no means a trivial matter. A great deal depends, first of all, on where the sample is actually taken from. If the sample is drawn from a stagnant side tap, or from a quiet corner where the effluent is barely moving, what ends up in the sample bottle may bear very little resemblance to the effluent that is flowing through the main line, and a sampling point located in a well-mixed, flowing part of the stream is therefore strongly to be preferred. Just as importantly, a single sample is not usually collected in one go; instead, one sample is built up from a number of separate increments that are taken over the period which the sample is intended to represent and then combined together. The number of increments that form one sample depends on how variable the stream is expected to be, with a more variable stream calling for more increments spread more widely across the period. A single grab sample, taken at one moment and in one place, can be seriously misleading, because the composition of an effluent stream changes over time as production varies and as batch operations come and go; a grab sample may catch the stream at an unusual peak or in an unrepresentative trough and then present that moment as if it were the whole picture. Finally, it should be noted that no numerical limits are quoted in this passage, since regulatory limits of that kind are set by the permit for the individual site rather than by any general discussion.
target: A sample of an effluent stream has one job: to stand for the stream over the period the result will be applied to. Representativeness is fixed by three choices, where the sample is taken, how its increments are spread, and what a single grab sample is never asked to do. The sampling point belongs in the flowing, mixed part of the stream. Effluent drawn from a stagnant side tap or a quiet corner of a channel has sat apart from the flow, and its composition is the composition of that corner, not of the discharge. A point in the main line, where the stream is moving and mixed, gives the increments a chance to match the stream they represent. One sample is built from increments. Each increment is a small portion taken at its own moment, and the increments are combined into the single sample that goes for analysis. How many increments form one sample follows the variability of the stream: a steady stream needs few, a stream that swings with production needs increments spread across the whole period, so that peaks and troughs enter the sample in proportion to their duration. A grab sample misleads by construction. One portion, taken at one moment, records the stream as it was at that moment, and an effluent stream changes from hour to hour as batches discharge and processes start and stop. The grab sample may land on a peak or in a trough and be reported as the stream's normal state. No numerical limits are quoted here; regulatory limits for an effluent are set in the permit for the site, and the permit is not part of this passage.
